result:
The proposed solution is wrong because its key step does not produce a full black square.

If the upper-left k×k block is black, the 2×2 square on rows k, k+1 and columns k, k+1 does have exactly one black cell, (k,k). Colouring the other three cells black does not make the upper-left (k+1)×(k+1) block black. The cells (1,k+1), …, (k−1,k+1) and (k+1,1), …, (k+1,k−1) are still white. So the induction fails, and "every n works" is unjustified.

A check on n = 3 shows it is false:

1. Start with (1,1) black. The only available move is the top-left 2×2 square, which makes (1,1), (1,2), (2,1), (2,2) black.
2. The squares at rows 1–2 with columns 2–3, and at rows 2–3 with columns 1–2, each contain two black cells, so they are not allowed.
3. The square at rows 2–3, columns 2–3 contains only (2,2), so it is allowed. It makes (2,3), (3,2), (3,3) black.
4. Now only (1,3) and (3,1) are white. The square at rows 1–2, columns 2–3 has three black cells, and the square at rows 2–3, columns 1–2 also has three black cells. No move is possible, so the 3×3 board cannot be completed.

Since n = 3 does not work, the set of valid n is not {1, 2, 3, …}, and the sum 210 is incorrect.

VERDICT: REJECT
